table.footnote: All rows are live/intraday, the publisher's own same-day close, or weekly-by-nature (mortgage, NFCI). The 2-year, 2s10s, real 10y and the two breakevens are the US Treasury's official curve for the last completed session — there is no intraday quote for a 2-year or for TIPS — so the slope is that session's 10-year less that session's 2-year, and will not exactly equal the intraday 10-year shown above it. Dollar (DXY) is the ICE dollar index. FX changes are signed from the dollar's perspective (+ = stronger dollar): EUR/USD and GBP/USD are dollars-per-foreign-unit, so their signs are flipped; DXY, USD/JPY, USD/CHF, USD/CAD and USD/CNY are already up = stronger dollar.

table.footnote: Core inflation is each country's own measure and the definitions differ. The United States is CPI less food and energy; Canada is Statistics Canada's CPI less food and energy (the Bank of Canada's own CPI-trim and CPI-median are a different definition and are not used here); the United Kingdom, the euro area, France, Germany and Italy are the harmonised index less energy, food, alcohol and tobacco; Japan is the CPI less fresh food (Japan's headline "core"). Brazil is the exception: it shows the IPCA-MS, Banco Central do Brasil's smoothed TRIMMED MEAN (SGS 4466), which excludes whatever moved most in a given month rather than a fixed list of items — so it is not strictly comparable with the cells above it. Brazil's own ex-food-and-energy core, the closest like-for-like measure, reads 4.6%. India's core is blank on purpose: it publishes no official core index. Japan's inflation comes from Japan's Statistics Dashboard, resolved to the current base year (the index rebases to a 2025 base in August 2026). The euro-area GDP figures cover all 21 members, including Croatia and Bulgaria; until 1 August 2026 they were drawn from a 19-member measure that predates both and read about 0.1 point lower.
